cell-structure-and-transport.title: Cell structure and transport
cell-structure-and-transport.about: Animal, plant and bacterial cells, microscopy and magnification, diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

questions.question: Which part of a cell contains the genetic material and controls the cell's activities?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the chromosomes, which carry the genetic material. It controls what the cell does. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.

questions.question: Bacterial cells are prokaryotic. Which statement about them is correct?
options: They are larger than most animal cells
Their DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus
Their cell wall is made of cellulose
questions.explanation: In prokaryotic cells the genetic material is a single loop of DNA in the cytoplasm, often with small rings called plasmids. They have no nucleus or mitochondria, are much smaller than animal cells, and their cell wall is not made of cellulose.

questions.question: Root hair cells take in mineral ions from the soil, where the ions are less concentrated than inside the cell. Which process is this?
questions.explanation: Moving substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated one is against the concentration gradient. This needs energy from respiration and is called active transport.

questions.question: A cell is 0.02 mm long. In a drawing of the cell it is 4 mm long. What is the magnification of the drawing?
questions.explanation: Magnification $= \dfrac{\text{size of image}}{\text{size of real object}} = \dfrac{4}{0.02} = 200$. Both lengths must be in the same unit before dividing.

questions.question: A cube of side 1 cm has a surface area of $6\ \text{cm}^2$ and a volume of $1\ \text{cm}^3$. A cube of side 2 cm has a surface area of $24\ \text{cm}^2$ and a volume of $8\ \text{cm}^3$. Which statement is correct?
options: The larger cube has the larger surface area to volume ratio
The smaller cube's surface area to volume ratio is twice that of the larger cube
Both cubes have the same surface area to volume ratio
The smaller cube's surface area to volume ratio is half that of the larger cube
questions.explanation: The smaller cube's ratio is 6 : 1 and the larger cube's is 24 : 8, which is 3 : 1. So the smaller cube's ratio is twice as large. This is why small organisms can rely on diffusion across their surface, while large ones need exchange surfaces and transport systems.

cell-division.title: Cell division
cell-division.about: Chromosomes, the cell cycle and mitosis, stem cells, meristems and bacterial growth.

questions.question: What name is given to undifferentiated cells that can develop into many different types of cell?
questions.explanation: Stem cells are undifferentiated. They can divide and then differentiate into specialised cells. They are found in embryos, in adult bone marrow and in plant meristems.

questions.question: Before a cell divides by mitosis, what happens to its DNA?
options: It is replicated, so there are two copies of each chromosome
questions.explanation: During the cell cycle the cell grows, makes more organelles and replicates its DNA. Each chromosome is copied so that each new cell receives a full set.

questions.question: Where are meristem cells found in a plant?
options: At the tips of the roots and shoots
questions.explanation: Meristem tissue at the tips of roots and shoots contains stem cells. These can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life.

questions.question: Mitosis is NOT used for which of these?
questions.explanation: Mitosis makes genetically identical cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Gametes such as sperm and egg cells are made by meiosis, which halves the number of chromosomes.

questions.question: A bacterium divides once every 20 minutes. Starting with a single bacterium, how many bacteria will there be after 2 hours, if none die?
questions.explanation: 2 hours is 120 minutes, which is $120 \div 20 = 6$ divisions. The number doubles each time, so there are $2^6 = 64$ bacteria.

organisation-and-digestion.title: Organisation and digestion
organisation-and-digestion.about: Levels of organisation, the digestive system, enzymes, food tests and plant tissues.

questions.question: Which list shows the levels of organisation from smallest to largest?
questions.explanation: Similar cells form a tissue, several tissues form an organ, and organs working together form an organ system.

questions.question: Which reagent is used to test a food for protein?
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple (lilac) if protein is present. Iodine tests for starch, Benedict's for sugars, and ethanol for lipids.

questions.question: What does bile do in digestion?
options: It digests proteins into amino acids
It neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats
It breaks down starch into sugars
questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is alkaline, so it neutralises stomach acid, and it emulsifies fats into small droplets, giving lipase a larger surface area to work on.

questions.question: Why does an enzyme stop working at a high temperature?
options: The shape of its active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits
It is killed by the heat
questions.explanation: High temperatures break bonds that hold the enzyme in shape. The active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits, so the enzyme is denatured. Enzymes are proteins, not living things, so they are not killed.

questions.question: Which change in conditions would increase the rate of transpiration from a plant?
questions.explanation: Moving air carries water vapour away from the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient, so water evaporates and diffuses out faster. Lower temperature, higher humidity and dimmer light all reduce the rate.

heart-blood-and-circulation.title: Heart, blood and circulation
heart-blood-and-circulation.about: The heart, blood vessels, components of blood and coronary heart disease.

questions.question: Which component of the blood carries oxygen?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen. They have no nucleus and a biconcave shape, giving more room and a larger surface area for oxygen.

questions.question: Why do arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls?
options: To withstand blood at high pressure
To let substances diffuse through them
Because they carry blood back to the heart
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Thick muscle and elastic fibres let them withstand and smooth out this pressure. Veins carry blood back to the heart and have valves.

questions.question: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood out to the rest of the body?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and around the body. It has the thickest wall because it must pump blood the furthest. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.

questions.question: Why is the human circulatory system described as a double circulatory system?
options: Blood flows in both directions in each vessel
Blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body
questions.explanation: One circuit takes blood from the heart to the lungs and back, and the other takes it from the heart to the rest of the body and back. So blood passes through the heart twice in each full circuit.

questions.question: In coronary heart disease, layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries. Why is this harmful?
options: It makes the heart beat faster
It makes the heart wall thicker
It stops the heart valves from closing
It reduces blood flow to the heart muscle, so the muscle gets less oxygen
questions.explanation: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood. If they narrow, less oxygen reaches the muscle, which can cause chest pain or a heart attack. Stents or statins can be used to treat it.

infection-and-response.title: Infection and response
infection-and-response.about: Pathogens and the diseases they cause, the body's defences, vaccination, antibiotics and drug trials.

questions.question: What type of pathogen causes malaria?
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by a protist. It is spread by mosquitoes, which act as vectors. Preventing mosquito bites, for example with nets, reduces the spread.

questions.question: How do some white blood cells help to defend the body against pathogens?
options: They carry oxygen to the pathogens
They form a clot over the pathogen
They release hormones that kill viruses
questions.explanation: White blood cells defend the body by engulfing pathogens (phagocytosis), producing antibodies, and producing antitoxins. Clotting is the job of platelets.

questions.question: How does a vaccine protect a person from a disease?
options: It contains antibiotics that kill the pathogen
It contains a dead or inactive form of the pathogen, so white blood cells make antibodies and memory cells
It contains antibodies taken from another person
It destroys viruses inside the body's cells
questions.explanation: The vaccine stimulates white blood cells to produce antibodies. Memory cells remain, so if the real pathogen enters later, antibodies are made quickly and the person does not become ill.

questions.question: Which of these diseases is caused by a bacterium?
questions.explanation: Salmonella food poisoning is caused by bacteria. Measles and HIV are caused by viruses, and rose black spot is caused by a fungus.

questions.question: In a double-blind trial of a new drug, who knows which patients are receiving the drug and which are receiving a placebo?
options: Both the doctors and the patients
Neither the doctors nor the patients
questions.explanation: In a double-blind trial neither the doctors nor the patients know who has the drug and who has the placebo until the end. This stops expectations from affecting the results.

photosynthesis.title: Photosynthesis
photosynthesis.about: The photosynthesis reaction, limiting factors, the inverse square law and how plants use glucose.

questions.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through the stomata.

questions.question: Why is photosynthesis described as an endothermic reaction?
options: Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light
questions.explanation: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings. In photosynthesis the energy is transferred by light and absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.

questions.question: On a warm, bright day the rate of photosynthesis of a plant stops increasing, even when the light gets brighter. Which factor is most likely to be limiting the rate?
questions.explanation: Light cannot be limiting, because making it brighter has no effect, and the day is already warm. Carbon dioxide concentration is the most likely limiting factor. Oxygen is a product, not a reactant.

questions.question: Plants turn some of the glucose they make into starch for storage. Why is starch useful for storage?
options: It is used directly to make proteins
It releases oxygen while it is stored
It is insoluble, so it does not draw water into cells by osmosis
questions.explanation: Starch is insoluble. Storing lots of soluble glucose would make cells draw in water by osmosis. Plants also use glucose for respiration, cellulose for cell walls, and with nitrate ions to make proteins.

questions.question: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm away from a plant. According to the inverse square law, what happens to the light intensity at the plant?
questions.explanation: Light intensity is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{d^2}$. Doubling the distance gives $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$ of the intensity.

respiration.title: Respiration
respiration.about: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration, fermentation, exercise, oxygen debt and metabolism.

questions.question: Where in a cell does most aerobic respiration take place?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration takes place mainly in the mitochondria. Cells that need a lot of energy, such as muscle and sperm cells, have many mitochondria.

questions.question: Which word equation shows aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose completely, producing carbon dioxide and water and transferring energy. The last equation is photosynthesis.

questions.question: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast cells?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration in yeast is called fermentation. It produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is why yeast is used in brewing and bread-making. Muscle cells make lactic acid instead.

questions.question: Why does anaerobic respiration transfer much less energy per molecule of glucose than aerobic respiration?
options: The oxidation of glucose is incomplete
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, glucose is only partly broken down, so much of its energy stays in the products such as lactic acid. Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely.

questions.question: After hard exercise, a person keeps breathing deeply and quickly for some time. Why?
options: To remove excess glucose from the blood
To repay the oxygen debt, supplying oxygen to break down lactic acid
questions.explanation: Lactic acid builds up during anaerobic respiration. The extra oxygen needed to deal with it is the oxygen debt. Blood carries the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.

homeostasis-and-hormones.title: Homeostasis and hormones
homeostasis-and-hormones.about: Homeostasis, the endocrine system, blood glucose and diabetes, reproductive hormones and plant hormones.

questions.question: Which gland is often called the 'master gland' because it releases hormones that control other glands?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland in the brain releases several hormones, such as FSH, LH and TSH, that act on other glands and cause them to release their own hormones.

questions.question: What is the cause of Type 1 diabetes?
options: Body cells stop responding to insulin
The liver makes too much glucagon
The pancreas produces little or no insulin
questions.explanation: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas produces too little insulin, so it is treated with insulin injections. In Type 2 diabetes the body's cells no longer respond properly to insulin.

questions.question: Which of these is an effect of the hormone adrenaline?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress. It increases heart rate, boosting the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles and preparing the body for 'fight or flight'.

questions.question: In the menstrual cycle, which hormone causes an egg to mature in the ovary?
questions.explanation: FSH (follicle stimulating hormone) from the pituitary gland causes an egg to mature. LH triggers ovulation, and oestrogen and progesterone build up and maintain the lining of the uterus.

questions.question: A person's blood glucose concentration falls too low. How does the body respond?
options: The pancreas releases insulin, so glucose moves into cells
The pancreas releases glucagon, so the liver converts glycogen into glucose
The kidneys release glucose into the urine
questions.explanation: When blood glucose is too low, the pancreas releases glucagon. This causes the liver to convert stored glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood. This is an example of negative feedback.

nervous-system.title: Nervous system
nervous-system.about: Neurones and reflex arcs, synapses, the brain and the eye.

questions.question: What does a sensory neurone do?
options: Carries impulses from the central nervous system to muscles
Connects neurones within the brain only
Carries impulses from receptors to the central nervous system
questions.explanation: Sensory neurones carry electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system. Motor neurones carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors.

questions.question: What is a synapse?
options: A type of receptor in the skin
The gap between two neurones, which is crossed by chemicals
The part of the brain that controls balance
A muscle that responds to impulses
questions.explanation: A synapse is a junction between two neurones. The impulse cannot jump the gap, so a chemical is released that diffuses across and starts an impulse in the next neurone.

questions.question: Why are reflex actions important?
options: They are slow and carefully thought about
They are rapid and automatic, which helps to protect the body
questions.explanation: Reflexes do not involve the conscious part of the brain, so they are very fast. Examples include pulling your hand away from something hot and the pupil narrowing in bright light.

questions.question: Which part of the eye controls how much light enters it?
questions.explanation: The iris contains muscles that change the size of the pupil. In bright light the pupil becomes smaller, letting less light in. The retina contains the light receptors.

questions.question: Which part of the brain controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing?
questions.explanation: The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing. The cerebral cortex is involved in memory, language and consciousness, and the cerebellum coordinates muscle activity and balance.

inheritance-and-genetics.title: Inheritance and genetics
inheritance-and-genetics.about: DNA and genes, meiosis, sexual and asexual reproduction, alleles and genetic crosses.

questions.question: What is a gene?
options: A small section of DNA that codes for a particular protein
All of an organism's genetic material
questions.explanation: A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome. It codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, which makes a specific protein. All of an organism's genetic material is its genome.

questions.question: What does it mean if a person is homozygous for a gene?
options: They have two different alleles of the gene
They have only one copy of each chromosome
They have a mutation in the gene
They have two identical alleles of the gene
questions.explanation: Homozygous means having two copies of the same allele, for example BB or bb. Heterozygous means having two different alleles, such as Bb.

questions.question: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human egg cell have?
questions.explanation: Gametes are made by meiosis, which halves the number of chromosomes. An egg cell has 23, so when it is fertilised by a sperm with 23, the embryo has the full 46.

questions.question: Which statement about sexual reproduction is correct?
options: It involves the fusion of male and female gametes, producing variation
It produces offspring that are clones of the parent
Its gametes are made by mitosis
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction joins genetic information from two parents when gametes fuse. The offspring are genetically different, which produces variation. Asexual reproduction needs one parent and produces clones.

questions.question: In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant to the allele for white flowers (p). A plant with genotype Pp is crossed with a plant with genotype pp. What percentage of the offspring are expected to have white flowers?
questions.explanation: The Pp parent gives P or p, and the pp parent always gives p. The offspring are Pp and pp in equal numbers. Only pp plants are white, so 50% are expected to be white.

variation-and-evolution.title: Variation and evolution
variation-and-evolution.about: Variation, mutation, natural selection, selective breeding, genetic engineering, fossils and classification.

questions.question: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.explanation: Charles Darwin published the theory of evolution by natural selection in 1859, based on his observations and experiments. Gregor Mendel carried out early work on inheritance using pea plants.

questions.question: Which of these characteristics is caused only by the environment?
questions.explanation: A scar results from something that happened to the person, so it is environmental. Blood group, eye colour and natural hair colour are inherited from the parents.

questions.question: What is selective breeding?
options: Animals choosing their own mates in the wild
Changing an organism's genes using enzymes
The survival of the best adapted organisms in nature
Humans choosing organisms with desired characteristics and breeding them together
questions.explanation: In selective breeding humans choose parents with a useful characteristic, breed them, and repeat over many generations. Changing genes with enzymes is genetic engineering, and survival of the best adapted is natural selection.

questions.question: Why is the fossil record incomplete?
options: Many early organisms were soft-bodied and left few traces
Fossils have only formed in the last thousand years
Only animals with backbones lived in the past
Every fossil that formed has been found
questions.explanation: Soft-bodied organisms rarely formed fossils, and many fossils have been destroyed by geological activity or have not yet been found. This is why scientists cannot be certain how life began.

questions.question: Bacteria can be genetically engineered to make human insulin. What is used as a vector to carry the human insulin gene into a bacterial cell?
questions.explanation: The gene is cut out using enzymes and inserted into a plasmid, a small ring of DNA. The plasmid carries the gene into the bacterium, which then makes insulin as it grows and divides.

ecology.title: Ecology
ecology.about: Food chains, biotic and abiotic factors, cycles of materials, biomass transfer and biodiversity.

questions.question: What is a producer in a food chain?
options: An organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis
An animal that eats other animals
An organism that breaks down dead material
questions.explanation: Producers, such as green plants and algae, make glucose by photosynthesis. They are always at the start of a food chain.

questions.question: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living, such as temperature, light intensity, moisture, soil pH and wind. Predation, pathogens and competition are biotic, because they involve living things.

questions.question: In the carbon cycle, how do decomposers return carbon to the atmosphere?
options: By respiring as they break down dead material, releasing carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi feed on dead organisms and waste. As they respire, they release carbon dioxide into the air, and mineral ions are returned to the soil.

questions.question: In a food chain, the producers have a biomass of 10 000 kg and the primary consumers have a biomass of 1000 kg. What is the efficiency of biomass transfer?
questions.explanation: Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{biomass transferred to the next level}}{\text{biomass available}} \times 100 = \dfrac{1000}{10\,000} \times 100 = 10\%$.

questions.question: In a predator-prey relationship, what usually happens soon after the number of prey increases?
options: The predator population stays exactly the same
questions.explanation: More prey means more food for the predators, so more of them survive and breed and their numbers rise. The predator peak comes a little after the prey peak.
